messages.subject: Delete calibrating masses from analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
i've a question. I'm analyzing some datasets where i'm using trypsin(842.508), angioII(1046.19) and glufib(1570.67) as internal calibrants when i scan the tissues.
I wonder if there is any way to delete them from the datasets just to avoid false positives or misleading predicting peaks.
Thanks in advance
Edu

messages.subject: Re: Delete calibrating masses from analysis
messages.body_plain:
You can use negative indexing as shown below. note this example works for peak data, not full mass range data.

#the features function will return the indices for an m/z or list of m/zs
calibrant_masses <- features(cardinaldata, mz=c(842.508, 1046.191,570.67))

#print dataset info
summary(cardinaldata)

Class: MSImageSet
Features: m/z = 501.26 ... m/z = 992.7 (344 total)

#the MSImageSet is organized msset[features, pixels]
#use negative index to remove features, shown below:

cardinaldata <- cardinaldata[-calibrant_masses,]

summary(cardinaldata)

Class: MSImageSet
Features: m/z = 501.26 ... m/z = 986.7 (341 total)

Alternatively, as a one-liner:
cardinaldata <- cardinaldata[-features(cardinaldata, mz=c(842.508, 1046.191,570.67)),]

a forewarning with picked peak data, check the ion images and line plots of the picked peak data at the masses of your calibrants a to ensure you are removing the calibrants and not an adjacent peak. The peak picking and alignment oftentimes will shift the mass of the peaks from the value you see in individual spectra. The features function will find the peak with the closet value to what you input in mz, so if there is significant shift, it may detect an adjacent peak rather than your calibrant.

Best of luck,
Heath

messages.subject: Regarding multiple datasets
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have one question regarding reading multiple data-sets simultaneously using Cardinal. I have several MSI datasets and I want to cluster them all together sothat I can compare different cluster classes obtained. Can you please tell me how I can read them in Cardinal or create single SIMageset contains all these sample files.

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: Regarding multiple datasets
messages.body_plain:
You can read them all in individually, here i'm using imzML as an example file

msset1 <- readImzML("msset1",folder=getwd())

msset2 <- readImzML("msset2",folder=getwd())

msset3 <- readImzML("msset3",folder=getwd())

to combine 2 datasets using Cardinal's combine function

msset1_2<- combine(msset1,msset2)

I'm not sure if this has changed or if it is an efficient way of doing it but to combine many I usually use the following
msset1_2_3 <- do.call(combine, list(msset1,msset2,msset3))

The combine function requires that the all m/z values be equal for continuous datasets and you may need a "sample" vector in your MSImageSet pixelData.

What I've typically done with large datasets is create a peak list that is common to all datasets, find those peaks in datasets individually, then combine the peak data into one file. If you are intrested in doing clustering, you will want to have some reduced dimension data anyway.

Maybe Kylie can give more info here.

Heath

messages.subject: Re: Regarding multiple datasets
messages.body_plain:
What Heath describes is still the most straightforward way, especially if the data are smaller or you have a machine with lots of memory.

If the datasets are large, combining them before peak picking may be difficult due to memory issues, so processing them as Heath describes to peak-picked data with matching m/z values is often preferred.

I am currently working on a better backend for larger datasets and improving batchProcess() to where it is easier to combine and process datasets without fully loading them into memory. I am *hoping* it will be ready for the next Bioconductor release next month, but don't want to promise that yet.

-Kylie
